title: Objects All the Way Down
body: PowerShell isn't just another command shell — every single thing a cmdlet returns is a real .NET object with its own properties and methods, not a wall of plain text you have to parse yourself. That one design choice is why cyber operators lean on it constantly: you can filter, sort, and pipe real data between commands with total precision, whether you're enumerating processes on a box or automating a security sweep across hundreds of machines.
keyPoints: PowerShell cmdlets follow a strict Verb-Noun pattern with a singular noun: Get-Process, never Get-Processes.
Windows 10 ships with PowerShell 5.1 by default; typing pwsh drops you into PowerShell 7.x side by side, and exit returns you to the previous session.

title: The Pipeline: Passing Objects, Not Text
body: Classic shells pipe raw text between commands, which means the receiving command has to re-parse that text to make sense of it. PowerShell's pipeline (|) passes whole objects instead — so a filter like Where-Object can reach directly into a real property on a real object, no string-parsing required. A typical pipeline reads left to right: get some objects, filter them down, keep only the properties you care about, then decide how to display the result.
keyPoints: Objects in PowerShell are passed through pipes based on their inputted cmdlets — the whole object travels, not just its printed text.
Format-Table and Format-List only change how the final result is displayed; they don't change the underlying objects.

title: Every Cmdlet Returns an Object — Prove It With Get-Member
body: Run Get-Process | Get-Member and PowerShell tells you exactly what you're holding: the object's TypeName (System.Diagnostics.Process) plus every property and method available on it. Properties are what you know about the object — Name, Id, Handles. Methods are what you can do to it — Kill(), Start(). That's why (Get-Process notepad).Kill() and Stop-Process -Name notepad both stop the same process: one calls the .NET method directly, the other is the cmdlet wrapper around it.
keyPoints: Get-Process | Get-Member | Where-Object {$_.Membertype -match "Method"} isolates just the methods, filtering out the properties.
Different object types expose completely different members — Get-EventLog -LogName System | Get-Member looks nothing like Get-Process | Get-Member.

title: Filtering With $_ and Where-Object
body: $_ is the pipelined variable — inside a Where-Object script block, it always means "the object currently passing through, from whatever came before it in the pipeline." Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq "Stopped"} reads naturally once you see it: for each service object flowing through, keep it only if its Status property equals "Stopped." There's also a shorthand form — Get-Service | where Status -eq "Stopped" — that skips the script block and $_ entirely but returns the exact same result.
keyPoints: $_ is always the same object type as whatever the previous pipeline stage produced.
The shorthand form is -Property -Operator Value, e.g. where Handles -GE 1000, with no curly braces or $_ needed.

title: Execution Policy: Restricted by Default
body: Because a .ps1 script can contain anything — including malicious code — PowerShell ships locked down. The default Execution Policy is Restricted, which blocks every script that wasn't created in the local intranet zone or a workgroup. Get-ExecutionPolicy -List shows the policy for every scope at once (Machine, User, Process...), and Set-ExecutionPolicy changes it for a given scope. This is exactly the kind of control a cyber operator needs to understand both to defend a box and to know what a compromised one might have quietly changed.

rows.label: Restricted
cells: Default. No scripts run at all — only individual interactive commands.

rows.label: AllSigned
cells: Scripts run only if signed by a trusted publisher.

rows.label: RemoteSigned
cells: Local scripts run freely; anything downloaded must be signed.

rows.label: Unrestricted
cells: All scripts run, with a warning shown for downloaded ones.

rows.label: Bypass
cells: Everything runs — nothing is blocked or warned about.

keyPoints: Restricted is the out-of-the-box default on a fresh Windows install.
Set-ExecutionPolicy -ExecutionPolicy Unrestricted -Scope CurrentUser changes the policy for just the current user, not the whole machine.

title: PowerShell Remoting: WinRM Replaces DCOM
body: PowerShell Remoting (since v2) lets you run commands on another machine entirely, using WinRM (Windows Remote Management) instead of the older DCOM. That's a deliberate security upgrade: WinRM needs only one firewall port open, defaults to Kerberos authentication, and encrypts every session with a per-session AES-256 key. Outside an Active Directory domain — or when connecting by raw IP address, which breaks Kerberos — you fall back to NTLM, and the target has to be explicitly added to the client's TrustedHosts list first.
keyPoints: WinRM defaults to port 5985 for HTTP and 5986 for HTTPS (which needs a certificate configured).
Setting TrustedHosts to "*" trusts every host on the network — fine for a quick lab test, a real security risk anywhere else.

title: Profiles: Making Aliases and Functions Stick
body: Create an alias or a function interactively and it vanishes the moment you close the window — by design, nothing persists automatically. A PowerShell profile is a plain .ps1 script, not created by default, that PowerShell checks for and runs automatically every time a matching session starts. There are four possible profiles, checked in order from lowest to highest precedence, so a setting in your own Current User, Current Host profile always wins over a machine-wide one.

steps.label: Current User, Current Host — highest precedence, yours alone

keyPoints: New-Item -ItemType File -Path $PROFILE -Force creates the Current User, Current Host profile if it doesn't exist yet.
$PROFILE | Get-Member -Type NoteProperty reveals the paths to all four possible profile files, even the ones that don't exist on disk.

title: Ready to Drill
body: You now have the core mental model: PowerShell moves real objects through a pipeline, every object exposes properties and methods you can inspect with Get-Member, Where-Object filters that pipeline with either a script block or shorthand syntax, Execution Policy locks scripts down by default, and Remoting/profiles extend all of it across sessions and machines. Head into the practice terminal and try the commands yourself before you drill — muscle memory sticks better than reading alone.
keyPoints: Verb-Noun cmdlets, singular nouns, dash-prefixed (or positional) parameters.
The pipeline passes whole objects, not text — Get-Member always tells you what you're holding.
$_ means "the current pipeline object"; Where-Object also has a shorthand -Property -Operator Value form.
Default Execution Policy is Restricted; WinRM (not DCOM) powers Remoting; profiles make customizations persistent.
